MUAR: Sixty-one doctors across generations of one family came together to bid a final farewell to their matriarch, Loo Siew Chin, who passed away at age 104.
The remarkable legacy of having so many doctors in the family began with Loo and her late husband, Lim Tang Too, who were rubber tappers in Muar, earning meagre wages.
Their daughter Karin Lim, 66, said a personal tragedy helped shape the couple’s determination after they lost a child to illness at a time when access to healthcare was difficult.
“That experience led to my father’s resolve to see his children become doctors so they could help others.
“Despite their humble background, my parents firmly held to their belief that education was the key to a better future,” she told The Star.
Karin said her eldest brother became a doctor, and the others started following in his footsteps.
Of the couple’s 11 children, eight sons became doctors, while another went into business.
Karin pursued law, and her sister became a housewife.
The family’s medical legacy has since grown to 61 doctors across the children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren and their spouses, with some younger family members still pursuing medicine at universities.
Karin, a lawyer based in Penang, said she had initially hoped to study medicine but decided to chart her own path.
“One of my brothers subsequently pointed out that there was no shortage of doctors, prompting me to pursue law instead,” she said.
Asked whether having so many doctors in the family could have contributed to her mother’s longevity, Lim said it might have helped but credited Loo’s strong character and resilience.
“She was a real fighter and had a strong character. We are who we are today because of her and my late father’s teachings,” she said, adding that her mother passed away peacefully on Nov 12.
Karin said more than 120 family members spanning several generations flew in from across Malaysia, as well as Singapore, Australia, Britain and Ireland to attend Loo’s funeral at Trinity Church Muar Cemetery yesterday.
She added that her parents had always wanted their descendants to thrive in their respective fields, but they equally emphasised the importance of staying close as a family.
“Since we are a big family, they always instilled in us the importance of being united and meeting during festive seasons and special occasions.
“That is the message we will carry with us. Now that both our parents are gone, we will take turns hosting reunions to keep the spirit of unity alive,” she said.

- Names must remain neutral regarding religion, politics, culture and gender.

- Higher Ocean Temperature: Warm ocean waters provide favourable conditions for cyclone development.
- Freshwater Inflow: Rivers such as the Ganga and Brahmaputra create a low-salinity surface layer that can reduce vertical ocean mixing.
- Atmospheric Disturbances: Weather systems originating over the western Pacific can contribute to cyclone formation.
- Favourable Wind Conditions: Relatively low vertical wind shear during the post-monsoon season supports cyclone development.
- Geographical Shape: The funnel-shaped northern Bay of Bengal increases vulnerability to storm surges.
Historically, the Bay of Bengal has experienced substantially more cyclones than the Arabian Sea.
- Post-Monsoon Conditions: Warm ocean temperatures and favourable atmospheric circulation support repeated cyclone formation.
- Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO): Its active phase can enhance cloud formation, rainfall and cyclonic activity.
- Ocean Heat Content: Heat stored beneath the ocean surface can sustain cyclone intensification.
- Atmospheric Waves: Equatorial Rossby and Kelvin waves can contribute to the development of low-pressure systems.
Climate change can influence the intensity and destructive potential of tropical cyclones through:
- Rising sea surface temperatures and ocean heat content.
- Increased atmospheric moisture leading to heavier rainfall.
- Rising sea levels increasing coastal flooding and storm surge risks.
- Greater potential for rapid intensification of cyclonic systems.
- Enables timely evacuation of vulnerable coastal populations.
- Reduces casualties and economic losses.
- Protects agriculture, fisheries and coastal infrastructure.
- Supports disaster preparedness and resource mobilisation.
- Strengthens maritime safety and port management.
- Agricultural Impact: Heavy rainfall, flooding and strong winds may damage standing crops, particularly paddy and horticultural crops.
- Economic Impact: Disruptions in fisheries, maritime trade, transportation and electricity supply could cause significant economic losses.
- Infrastructure Damage: Strong winds may damage roads, electrical infrastructure, communication networks and vulnerable houses.
- Environmental Impact: Coastal flooding, soil salinisation, beach erosion and damage to coastal ecosystems may occur.
- Humanitarian Impact: Displacement, loss of livelihoods and disruption of essential services may increase the vulnerability of coastal communities.

IMD weather update: ‘Yellow’ alert issued for Andhra, Odisha as Cyclone Akvan turns ‘very severe’ ahead of landfall
Cyclone Akvan is very likely to intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm around 19 November morning and cross Andhra Pradesh between Nellore and Tuni around noon the next day, said the IMD.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued a “yellow alert” for Andhra Pradesh and adjoining South Odisha coasts as Cyclone Akvan, currently a deep depression in the Bay of Bengal, intensifies.
This is the third cyclonic storm formed over the Bay of Bengal in three weeks.
The weather agency said that a deep depression over the southeast and adjoining southwest Bay of Bengal moved at a speed of 10 kmph during the past six hours till 5.30 pm and intensified into the cyclonic storm Akvan.
It lay centred at a distance of 790 km south of Gopalpur in Odisha.
It is very likely to intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm around 19 November morning and cross Andhra Pradesh between Nellore and Tuni around noon the next day, with a maximum sustained wind speed of 120-130 kmph, gusting to 145 kmph, the IMD said.
The IMD has placed multiple states on high alert, mapping out a massive footprint of extreme weather and tidal surges across the eastern and central regions:
Coastal Andhra Pradesh: Expected to bear the brunt of the storm, the region will see heavy showers begin on 18 November, rapidly escalating to isolated extremely heavy rainfall (≥21 cm) on 19 and 20 November.
A dangerous storm surge of 1.0 to 1.5 metres above the astronomical tide is forecast to inundate low-lying areas across Prakasam, Bapatla, Krishna, West Godavari, Konaseema, and Kakinada districts during landfall. Authorities warn that the peak surge will specifically hit Bapatla, Krishna and West Godavari districts.
Odisha & Rayalaseema: Odisha will experience escalating downpours, starting with heavy rain on 18 November and peaking with heavy to very heavy rainfall from 19 to 21 November. Rayalaseema is also on alert for heavy showers on 19 and 20 November.
West Bengal: The storm is likely to bring heavy rain to South 24 Parganas, Purba Medinipur, Paschim Medinipur and Jhargram districts from 19 to 21 November. The system will also cause thunderstorms, accompanied by gusty winds, over most districts of south Bengal, including the state capital, Kolkata, the Met Department said.
Tamil Nadu, Puducherry & Karaikal: The region is forecast to receive heavy to very heavy rainfall at isolated places on 18 and 19 November, alongside broader moderate showers continuing through 20 November.
Inland & Eastern Regions: As the system tracks inland, Eastern Telangana will face heavy to very heavy rainfall on 20 November. Neighbouring areas, including South and North Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Vidarbha, East Madhya Pradesh, and Gangetic West Bengal, are forecast to experience isolated heavy showers between 19 and 21 November.
Odisha is likely to receive "heavy rainfall, but not extremely heavy rainfall" as experienced during Cyclone Arnab, which made landfall in Andhra Pradesh on 28 October, IMD Director General Mrutunjay Mohapatra said.
"The impact of Cyclone Akvan is likely to be less on Odisha than that of Cyclone Arnab. We have not issued any red warning of extremely heavy rainfall this time," Bhubaneswar Meteorological Centre Director Manorama Mohanty said.
The Met office issued orange (rainfall between 12 cm and 20 cm) and yellow (rainfall between 7 cm and 11 cm) warnings for various districts in Odisha between 18 and 21 November, she said.

IMD issues orange alert for Chennai, Tiruvallur and Chengalpattu as Cyclone Akwan nears coast
The IMD has issued an orange alert for Chennai, Tiruvallur and Chengalpattu on November 18 and 19 as a Bay of Bengal deep depression strengthens into Cyclone Akwan, bringing extremely heavy rain before its November 20 Andhra Pradesh landfall.
Chennai: A layer of smog blankets several areas of the Tamil Nadu capital.
New Delhi: Residents across northern Tamil Nadu are bracing for wet weather as the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued an orange alert for Chennai, Tiruvallur, and Chengalpattu on November 18 and 19. The warning comes in response to a deep depression currently brewing over the southeast and adjoining southwest Bay of Bengal, according to a report by Dinamalar.
The weather system has been moving steadily in a north-northwest direction at a speed of roughly 6 kmph over the last six hours. Weather officials tracking the system expect it to gain further strength and turn into a very severe cyclonic storm, named Akwan, before it makes landfall.
The cyclone is projected to cross the Andhra Pradesh coast somewhere between Nellore and Tuni on November 20. At the time of landfall, wind speeds are expected to pick up significantly, reaching 120 to 130 kmph with gusts going up to 145 kmph.
Heavy rain likely to disrupt daily life in Chennai
For the three northern Tamil Nadu districts, the orange alert specifically flags the possibility of extremely heavy rainfall across both November 18 and 19. Alongside the intense downpours, general heavy rain is also expected in the region during this two-day window.
This forecast carries weight for the Chennai metropolitan region, which features densely populated neighbourhoods, busy road networks, and several low-lying pockets. Sustained rain in these areas could easily slow down road traffic, affect public transport schedules, and put pressure on regular urban services. However, the exact amount of expected rainfall, potential waterlogging zones, or specific advisories from civic and disaster-management bodies have not been detailed yet.
Rough sea warning for fishermen
Beyond the rain forecast on land, the weather department has also flagged rough sea conditions for November 17 and 18. Fishermen along the coast have been strictly advised against venturing out into the waters, while those already out at sea have been urged to return to the shore safely.
With the system inching closer, local administrations, coastal communities, and everyday commuters in Chennai, Tiruvallur, and Chengalpattu remain on watch. All eyes are now on the storm’s path toward Andhra Pradesh, the rainfall intensity over the next two days, and its eventual landfall on November 20.

Chennai and neighbouring districts in Tamil Nadu are expecting heavy rainfall as Cyclone Akvan makes a grip over the Bay of Bengal and is now moving towards the Andhra Pradesh coast.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall at isolated places across north Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal on November 18 and 19.
An orange alert has been issued for Chennai, Tiruvallur and Chengalpattu for both days, and the department has warned the residents to prepare for intense showers, thunderstorms.
Cyclone Akvan Latest Update
According to the IMD's National Bulletin, issued at 5:45 AM on November 17, Cyclone Akvan was currently over the central parts of the south and adjoining westcentral Bay of Bengal at 2:30 AM. It was located approximately 610 km east of Chennai. The weather is expected to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm around the evening of November 17 and further move into a very severe cyclonic storm around the morning of November 19.
The IMD expects the cyclone to move northwestwards and cross the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between Nellore and Tuni around noon on November 20. At landfall, it could have maximum sustained wind speeds of 120-130 kmph, with gusts reaching 145 kmph.
Chennai Rain Alert: Districts Under Orange And Yellow Warnings
The IMD has forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall at isolated places over north Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal on November 18 and 19.
Chennai, Tiruvallur and Chengalpattu are among the districts under orange alert. Residents should monitor local weather updates and prepare for possible waterlogging and traffic disruption.
The cyclone's impact is also expected across neighbouring states. Coastal Andhra Pradesh may receive heavy to very heavy rainfall, with isolated extremely heavy rainfall on November 19 and 20. Odisha is also likely to receive heavy to very heavy rainfall at isolated places between November 19 and 21.
Even sea conditions along the north Tamil Nadu and Puducherry coasts are likely to be rough to very rough until November 20. IMD has advised fishermen to not venture into the affected areas of the Bay of Bengal during the warning period.
Will Schools Be Closed In Chennai?
Despite the cyclonic intensity on the surge, there is no official announcement of a school or college holiday in Chennai. Parents and students should check announcements from the Tamil Nadu government, district administration and respective educational institutions before making plans.
